name: Divine right of kings
summary: The divine right of kings holds that monarchy is a divinely ordained institution, that the king's title comes from God and by hereditary succession rather than from the people, that kings answer to God alone and cannot be limited or judged by parliaments or subjects, and that subjects owe non-resistance and passive obedience.
scope: The Western Christian doctrine of divine-right monarchy as Figgis (s1) and Britannica (s3) define it: early modern (16th-17th century) royal absolutism in England, Scotland and France, with its roots in the medieval idea that God awards temporal power to the ruler. It covers James VI and I's Trew Law of Free Monarchies and Basilikon Doron (s2), Barclay's De Regno, Filmer's Patriarcha and Bossuet's Politique (s4), and the four propositions Figgis lists: monarchy divinely ordained, hereditary right indefeasible, kings accountable to God alone, non-resistance enjoined by God. It excludes other doctrines of divinely backed rulers (sacred kingship, the Mandate of Heaven, God emperors), which Wikipedia's hatnote sends elsewhere, and the 'divine right' of church government, which the books found under the redirect names treat.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: The doctrine makes the king's hereditary right indefeasible (Figgis, s1, Introductory, p. 5), so abolishing hereditary rank would abolish the kingship it defends.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Figgis (s1, Introductory, p. 6) has the king's power incapable of legal limitation with assemblies existing at his pleasure, so a legislature's prior approval of spending cannot bind him.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Figgis (s1, Introductory, p. 6) quotes the doctrine that kings derive their title not from the people but from God and that it is not for subjects to create or censure them.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Figgis (s1, Introductory, p. 6) says all constitutional forms and assemblies exist at the king's pleasure, so an elected assembly writing the constitution is excluded.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Under the doctrine the king holds the throne by indefeasible hereditary right and subjects have no part in creating him (Figgis, s1, Introductory), which excludes choosing him by popular vote.

direct-votes.rationale: Filmer (s6, Free-holders Grand Inquest, p. 10) holds the legislative power proper to the king, and Figgis (s1, Introductory, p. 6) calls all law a concession of his will, which leaves no lawmaking by popular vote.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Figgis (s1, Introductory) gives the doctrine's first proposition as monarchy being a divinely ordained institution, and Britannica (s3) says kings derived their authority from God.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Figgis (s1, Introductory, p. 5) states that hereditary right is indefeasible and succession follows primogeniture, which cannot be forfeited by usurpation or deposition.

elective-rulers.rationale: Figgis (s1, Introductory, p. 5) quotes the doctrine that kings derive their title not from the people but from God, by fundamental hereditary right, so subjects do not create the king.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Figgis (s1, Introductory, p. 6) says the king's power is incapable of legal limitation and constitutional forms exist at his pleasure, which rules out a charter binding him.

head-of-state-dissolves-parliament.rationale: Figgis (s1, Introductory, p. 6) says assemblies exist entirely at the king's pleasure, and Filmer (s6, Free-holders Grand Inquest, p. 10) has the king's power over Parliament as source of its acts.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Figgis (s1, Introductory, p. 6) says a mixed or limited monarchy is a contradiction in terms, and Filmer (s6, Anarchy of a Limited or Mixed Monarchy) argues the same.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Filmer (s6, Free-holders Grand Inquest, p. 9-10) argues the legislative power is proper to the king, and Figgis (s1, Introductory, p. 6) says assemblies exist at the king's pleasure.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Figgis (s1, Introductory, p. 6) says resistance to a king is a sin even when he commands against God's law, where subjects are to endure the penalties patiently.

resist-oppression-despite-death.rationale: The doctrine's non-resistance proposition (Figgis, s1, Introductory, p. 6) tells subjects to endure penalties patiently rather than resist, even when the king commands against God's law.

revolution-legitimate.rationale: Figgis (s1, Introductory, p. 6) gives non-resistance as the fourth proposition: under any circumstances resistance to a king is a sin that ensures damnation.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Britannica's account of Bossuet (s3) has the doctrine assert that the king's person and authority are sacred, and James's Basilikon Doron (s5, opening Sonnet) calls kings God's lieutenants sitting on his throne.

separated-powers.rationale: Figgis (s1, Introductory, p. 6) says the sovereignty is entirely vested in the king and cannot be limited or divided, and Filmer (s6, Anarchy of a Limited or Mixed Monarchy, p. 266) calls a supreme limited power a contradiction.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Figgis (s1, Introductory, p. 5-6) says the king's power is incapable of legal limitation and all law is a concession of his will; Britannica (s3) says he cannot be held accountable by any earthly authority.

state-harmful.rationale: Figgis (s1, Introductory, p. 7-8) lists the scriptural texts the doctrine rests on, such as that the powers that be are ordained of God, so the government is to be obeyed, not abolished.

notes: Themes searched: government (sovereignty, parliament, succession, resistance), religion (source of authority, sacred ruler), liberty and law. Figgis's Introductory chapter, Britannica, James's Basilikon Doron (Morley) and Filmer (Free-holders Grand Inquest and Anarchy of a Limited or Mixed Monarchy) were read. Statements on economy, society, world and technology are null: the sources are silent. The other books found under the redirect names concern church government, not kingship.
